    Field site example: Bemidji oil pipeline burst¶

    This notebooks outlines analysis of a contaminated field site near Bemidji (Minnesota, USA). It focusses on the analysis of the plume length under steady state conditions.

    Authors: Jorrit Bakker, Alraune Zech

    Site description¶

    Near the town of Bemidji, a crude-oil pipeline burst in 1979, releasing approximately \(1700 m^3\) of crude oil. After initial remediation efforts, about \(400 m^3\) of crude-oil remained in the soil.

    The subsurface consists of glacial outwash deposits, comprised of poorly sorted sandy gravel, gravely sand and sand interbedded with thin silt layers. This aquifer is underlain by a low permeable till layer\(^1\).

    A bromide tracer test performed in 1997\(^2\) between two wells (\(1.6m\) apart) calculated a flow velocity of \(0.06m/day\) and an estimated longitudinal dispersivity of \(\alpha_l = 0.15m\). As the tracer test was performed over a short distance, this values is not necessarily representing macro-dispersivity, but the actual longitudinal macrodispersivity is expected to be higher. No information is given on transverse horizontal or transverse vertical dispersivities. Observed average porosity is \(0.38\). The velocity determined by the tracer test is close to the range of \(0.004 - 0.056 m/day\) which reflects calculated velocity based on measured hydraulic gradients and hydraulic conductivities.

    Model setup¶

    Goal is to setup a transient transport model for the contaminant transport at the Bemidji site using field site characteristics and reproduce the steady state plume distribution/length as done by Köhler et al., 2026\(^4\).

    Hydrogeological parameters¶

    We chose hydraulic parameters following the site description. In this analysis, we assumed that \(\alpha_{th} = \alpha_l / 10\) and \(\alpha_{tv} = \alpha_l / 100\). Although these are rough estimates, they correspond with reasonable orders of magnitude for the respective parameters\(^3\).

    Attenuation and fringe degradation parameters¶

    For biodegradation, we first model it using only fringe degradation. Therefore, we assume a decay rate of 0. As the example looks at steady state, and therefore disregard contaminant retardation. Retardation only influences the time until steady state is reached, not the concentration distribution at steady state.

    Following Köhler et al., 2026\(^4\), we use only one electron acceptor, oxygen, with a concentration of \(8 g/m^3\) and a single electron donor: benzene. Biodegradation reaction stoichiometry gives 1:7.5 for Benzene:Oxygen\(^7\).

    Source conditions¶

    No source depletion is considered, since that is incompatible with steady state conditions. We use a source concentration of \(6 g/m^3\) and a source dimensions of \(1m\) following \(^{1,4}\) Note that Bekins et al., 2016\(^5\) reports initial source concentrations in the range of \(4-7 g/m^3\) which is close to the values we use.

    Model parameters¶

    We model the plume within a distance of 200m and a total of \(10\) years.

    References¶

    \(^1\) Essaid, H. I., Bekins, B. A., Herkelrath, W. N., & Delin, G. N. (2011). Crude Oil at the Bemidji Site: 25 Years of Monitoring, Modeling, and Understanding. Groundwater, 49(5), 706–726.

    \(^2\) Essaid, H. I., Cozzarelli, I. M., Eganhouse, R. P., Herkelrath, W. N., Bekins, B. A., & Delin, G. N. (2003). Inverse modeling of BTEX dissolution and biodegradation at the Bemidji, MN crude-oil spill site. Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, 67(1), 269–299.

    \(^3\) Zech, A., Attinger, S., Bellin, A., Cvetkovic, V., Dietrich, P., Fiori, A., Teutsch, G. & Da-gan, G. (2019). A critical analysis of transverse dispersivity field data. Groundwater 57 (4), 632–639.

    \(^4\) Köhler, A. V., Craig, J. R., Yadav, P. K., & Liedl, R. (2026). An Analytic Element Method solution for simulating multiple steady-state groundwater contamination scenarios. Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, 276, 104733.

    \(^5\) Bekins, B. A., Cozzarelli, I. M., Erickson, M. L., Steenson, R. A., & Thorn, K. A. (2016).Crude Oil Metabolites in Groundwater at Two Spill Sites. Groundwater, 54(5), 681–691.

    \(^6\) Wiedemeier, T. H., Rifair, H. S., Newell, C. J., & Wilson, J. T. (1999). Intrinsic Bioremediation of Petroleum Hydrocarbons. In Natural Attenuation of Fuels and Chlorinated Solvents in the Subsurface (pp. 189–240). John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.

    \(^7\) Essaid, H. I., Cozzarelli, I. M., Eganhouse, R. P., Herkelrath, W. N., Bekins, B. A., & Delin, G. N. (2003). Inverse modeling of BTEX dissolution and biodegradation at the Bemidji, MN crude-oil spill site. Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, 67(1), 269–299.

    Modelling¶

    Use Mibitrans solution with fringe degradation for (aerobic) biodegradation to calculate the concentration distribution.

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    mbt_bemidji = mbt.Mibitrans(hydro, att, source, model)
mbt_bemidji.fringe_degradation(ea, 78)
results_bemidji = mbt_bemidji.run()
    mbt_bemidji = mbt.Mibitrans(hydro, att, source, model) mbt_bemidji.fringe_degradation(ea, 78) results_bemidji = mbt_bemidji.run()

plt.ylim([-2,2])

    Out[10]:

    Interpretation: The modelled plume length is \(159m\). This is only slightly more than the measured extend of \(150m\), also modelled by Köhler et al, 2026\(^4\).

    Disclaimer: Given the parameter estimations, and model assumptions, the modelling results are by no means conclusive.

    Core-Fringe-degradation¶

    Essaid et al. (2003)\(^7\) reported an anaerobic linear degradation rate of \(0.00065 day^{-1}\), estimated by inverse modeling using field measurements of the Bemedji site.

    In the following we test the effect of combining fringe-degradation reflecting aerobic degradation and anaerobic core-degradation based on input parameters from literature. Effectively, we combine the fringe degradation model as defined above with an anaerobic linear degradation rate of \(0.00065 day^{-1}\) into a core-fringe degradation model.

    In [11]:
    Copied! 
    att_cf= mbt.AttenuationParameters(
    decay_rate=0.00065, #[1/day]
    retardation=1 #[-]
)
mbt_bemidji_cf = mbt.Mibitrans(hydro, att_cf, source, model)
mbt_bemidji_cf.fringe_degradation(ea, 78)
results_bemidji_cf = mbt_bemidji_cf.run()
    att_cf= mbt.AttenuationParameters( decay_rate=0.00065, #[1/day] retardation=1 #[-] ) mbt_bemidji_cf = mbt.Mibitrans(hydro, att_cf, source, model) mbt_bemidji_cf.fringe_degradation(ea, 78) results_bemidji_cf = mbt_bemidji_cf.run()
    In [12]:
    Copied! 
    for i,plot_time in enumerate([5, 4, 3, 2, 1]):
    results_bemidji_cf.centerline(time=plot_time*365,
                               color=colors[i+1],lw=4-i*0.5,
                               label=f"t={plot_time}y")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
    for i,plot_time in enumerate([5, 4, 3, 2, 1]): results_bemidji_cf.centerline(time=plot_time*365, color=colors[i+1],lw=4-i*0.5, label=f"t={plot_time}y") plt.legend() plt.show()
    In [13]:
    Copied! 
    plume_length_index = np.argmin(results_bemidji_cf.cxyt[0][-1,len(results_bemidji_cf.y)//2,:])
print("Plume length is", results_bemidji_cf.x[plume_length_index], "m")
    plume_length_index = np.argmin(results_bemidji_cf.cxyt[0][-1,len(results_bemidji_cf.y)//2,:]) print("Plume length is", results_bemidji_cf.x[plume_length_index], "m")
    Plume length is 73 m

    Interpretation

    Combining both degradation modes using literature values results in a steady-state contaminant plume that is much shorter than the observed plume length. Consequently, degradation is overestimated.

    Assumptions

    The reason for the poor model fit can be explained when re-evaluating some of the model assumptions made:

    • Benzene was considered the only contaminant, despite the presence of other PHC. Consequently, it is very likely that oxygen was not only consumed by benzene degradation and consequently effect fringe degradation was overestimated.
    • The decay rate was fitted from observation but was not an absolute/measured parameter.
    • The model used literature estimates for transverse dispersivity independent of the specific field conditions.

    Degradation Scenarios¶

    Evaluating the model assumptions shows that three important input parameters of the model are uncertain: (i) decay rate representing anaerobic degradation,(ii) oxygen concentration available for benzene degradation, and (iii) transverse dispersivity.

    We will test the impact of these parameters and evaluate which parameter combinations are able to provide a plume length estimate that is close to the observed steady state plume length of 150m.

    Anearobic decay rates¶

    We test 5 values of anearobic degradation rates, ranging from the value reported by Essaid et al. (2003)\(^7\), of \(0.00065 day^{-1}\), down to one percent of that value.

    We stick to an oxygen concentration of \(8 g/m^3\) and a transverse dispersivity of \(\alpha_T = 0.015m\).

    In [14]:
    Copied! 
    decay_rates = [0.00065, 0.00065/2, 0.00065/5, 0.00065/10, 0.00065/100]
for i, decay_rate in enumerate(decay_rates):
    att_cf_low= mbt.AttenuationParameters(
        decay_rate=decay_rate, #[1/day]
        retardation=1 #[-]
    )
    mbt_bemidji_c_low_f = mbt.Mibitrans(hydro, att_cf_low, source, model)
    mbt_bemidji_c_low_f.fringe_degradation(ea, 78)
    results_bemidji_c_low_f = mbt_bemidji_c_low_f.run()
    results_bemidji_c_low_f.centerline(label = r"$\mu=$"fr"${decay_rate}$"r"$d^{-1}$",
                                       color=colors[i+1] ,lw = 2.25)
plt.title("Bemidji centerline with varying decay rate")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
    decay_rates = [0.00065, 0.00065/2, 0.00065/5, 0.00065/10, 0.00065/100] for i, decay_rate in enumerate(decay_rates): att_cf_low= mbt.AttenuationParameters( decay_rate=decay_rate, #[1/day] retardation=1 #[-] ) mbt_bemidji_c_low_f = mbt.Mibitrans(hydro, att_cf_low, source, model) mbt_bemidji_c_low_f.fringe_degradation(ea, 78) results_bemidji_c_low_f = mbt_bemidji_c_low_f.run() results_bemidji_c_low_f.centerline(label = r"$\mu=$"fr"${decay_rate}$"r"$d^{-1}$", color=colors[i+1] ,lw = 2.25) plt.title("Bemidji centerline with varying decay rate") plt.legend() plt.show()

    Oxygen concentation for Benzene degradation¶

    We test 5 values of oxygen concentration, ranging from the measured value of \(8 g/m^3\), down to \(1 g/m^3\). Note, that we do not question the well documented observed oxygen concentration, but reduce the value used in the model to reflect oxygen consumption by other contaminants reducing oxygen availability for modelled benzene degradation.

    We stick to the anaerobic degradation rate of \(0.00065 day^{-1}\) and a transverse dispersivity of \(\alpha_T = 0.015m\).

    In [16]:
    Copied! 
    ea_conc = [8,6,4,2,1]

    ea_low = mbt.ElectronAcceptors(
        electron_acceptor_concentration=eac,
        stoichiometric_ratio=7.5,
        electron_acceptor_molecular_weight=32,
    )
    mbt_bemidji_c_low_f = mbt.Mibitrans(hydro, att_cf, source, model)
    mbt_bemidji_c_low_f.fringe_degradation(ea_low, 78)
    results_bemidji_c_low_f = mbt_bemidji_c_low_f.run()
    results_bemidji_c_low_f.centerline(label=r"$C_{ea}="fr"${eac}$""g/m^{3}$",
                                       color=colors[i+1] ,lw = 2.25)
plt.title("Bemidji centerline with varying ea concentration")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

    Transverse Dispersivity¶

    We test 5 values of transverse dispersivity ranging from \(0.015m\) down to \(0.0015m\). Note that plume length is highly sensitive towards transverse dispersivity.

    We stick to an oxygen concentration of \(8 g/m^3\) and an anaerobic degradation rate of \(0.00065 day^{-1}\).

    In [18]:
    Copied! 
    transverse_h_disps = [0.015,0.01,0.006,0.003,0.0015]
for i, a_th in enumerate(transverse_h_disps):
    hydro_low = mbt.HydrologicalParameters(
        velocity=0.06, #[m/d]
        porosity=0.38, #[-]
        alpha_x=0.15, #[m]
        alpha_y=a_th, #[m]
        alpha_z=0.0015 #[m]
    )
    mbt_bemidji_low_cf = mbt.Mibitrans(hydro_low, att_cf, source, model)
    mbt_bemidji_low_cf.fringe_degradation(ea, 78)
    results_bemidji_low_cf = mbt_bemidji_low_cf.run()
    results_bemidji_low_cf.centerline(label=r"$\alpha_y=$"fr"${a_th}m$",
                                      color=colors[i+1] ,lw = 2.25)

    results_bemidji_low_cf.transverse(x_position=60, label=r"$\alpha_y=$"fr"${a_th}m$",
                                      color=colors[i+1] ,lw = 2.25)
plt.legend()
plt.title("Bemedji transverse (x=60m) with varying transverse horizontal dispersivity")
plt.ylim(0,4)
plt.show()
    transverse_h_disps = [0.015,0.01,0.006,0.003,0.0015] for i, a_th in enumerate(transverse_h_disps): hydro_low = mbt.HydrologicalParameters( velocity=0.06, #[m/d] porosity=0.38, #[-] alpha_x=0.15, #[m] alpha_y=a_th, #[m] alpha_z=0.0015 #[m] ) mbt_bemidji_low_cf = mbt.Mibitrans(hydro_low, att_cf, source, model) mbt_bemidji_low_cf.fringe_degradation(ea, 78) results_bemidji_low_cf = mbt_bemidji_low_cf.run() results_bemidji_low_cf.transverse(x_position=60, label=r"$\alpha_y=$"fr"${a_th}m$", color=colors[i+1] ,lw = 2.25) plt.legend() plt.title("Bemedji transverse (x=60m) with varying transverse horizontal dispersivity") plt.ylim(0,4) plt.show()

    Parameter combinations¶

    On trail-and-error basis, we determined 3 model scenarios that have different parameter combinations, but all happen to produce a steady state plume length of 150m that is in line with observed plume length.

    Conclusion¶

    All parameter combinations produced plumes with a length of 150 m, although plume shapes varied substantially. The available results do not allow us to determine which model configuration best represents field conditions. Nevertheless, the scenarios demonstrate how mibitrans can be used to conduct sensitivity analyses of input parameters.
